text: Good afternoon. This is April Chandler, and I call to order this November 12th, 2026 Select Committee of the school board regarding the MOU between LCPS, LCSO, and LPD. First up, we'll start with the approval of the minutes from the last meeting. Has everyone had an opportunity to review the minutes? I have that. Okay. I'll now entertain a motion.

Madam Chair, I move to approve the minutes from the last meeting. Vice Chair Donahue has moved to approve the minutes from the last meeting. Is there a second? Second. Thank you, Mr. Svendsen. Is there any discussion? All right. All those in favor of approving the minutes from the last meeting, please raise your hand and say aye. Aye. Aye. Aye. All right. That motion passes unanimously.

All right. We'll move on now to item number three on our agenda, and that's public comment. These are the procedures for public comment. Thank you for engaging with the school board through the public comment process. The school board welcomes comments from Loudoun County residents and believes that strong community engagement and outreach are important components of a successful school system. Speakers must limit comments to the time allotted. Based on the number of speakers in the agenda this evening, all speakers have been allotted two minutes each for public comment.

Please be advised that speakers who miss their time slot will not be called at a later time. All audience members shall maintain civility, decorum, and respect for the functioning and dignity of the school board at all times. Please remain seated unless arriving, departing, speaking at the podium, or during a break. Violations of civility, decorum, and respect include shouting, heckling, jeering, applause, and other noise which disrupts or delays the meeting, obstructing speakers from being able to see the school board and vice versa,

interrupting speakers attempting to speak when not called to do so by the chair, and approaching a speaker or otherwise attempting to intimidate, disparage, or distract a speaker, staff member, or other meeting attendees. Speakers should refrain from vulgarity, obscenities, defamation, profanity, and other like breaches of respect, nor may speakers target, criticize, or attack individual students or individual division employees during public comment. The school board requests that comments of an individual student or employee-related matter not be shared at public meetings where the

disclosure could violate applicable confidentiality requirements. The speaker should communicate those concerns to their school principal or another appropriate school official. Speakers should face the dais and direct their comments to the school board. Per school board policy 2520, members of the school board will not answer questions or respond directly to the public during the public comment period. To the extent necessary, I will warn of breaches of decorum, civility, and respect from attendees prior to taking other actions to preserve the orderly

conduct of the meeting. Violations of decorum, civility in other meeting attendees may result in the chair directing staff to remove the attendee from the remainder of the meeting. Repeated or persistent violations of decorum or civility by the audience may result in, on the decision of the chair, public comment being tabled until a later point in the meeting's agenda, limiting the number of attendees in the meeting room during public comment for safety reasons, or a public comment period ending for the evening.

Distribution of materials to school board members. Copies of materials for board members should be given to the public information officer in the media box at the back of the boardroom before the start of the meeting. Please provide 12 copies. Under no circumstances may a speaker approach the dais. The public is reminded that access to the school board meeting is available through LCPS-TV on 1070 HD and Verizon Fios channel 43. The live stream of the meeting may be viewed on the website. We look forward to hearing your comments. Our only speaker this afternoon is Amy Ricardi.

Ms. Ricardi, the floor is yours. Thank you, Madam Chair. I just wanted to say, I've had a chance to take a look at the MOU drafts and redlines that we've had before us to consider for the school board right now, and I understand the direction that Sheriff Chapman has gone with his MOU draft, and I was reminded as a business owner,

when I don't have a client or I have a client that has taken a long time to do a renewal, sometimes you just have to craft it and then give it to them and let them have a chance to respond to it and work from there. I'm really hoping that we can take a look at the documents that we have before us and get to a quick resolution and come up with the right solution that's in compliance with the current Virginia code. It is noted, I don't believe that the current version that we've got addresses elementary school SROs.

I know that the sheriff has put forth a recommendation and a proposal to the board of supervisors, which is a phased in approach, and I think that's a very wise one. I think when you get feedback from the public, in general, and you take out the both ends of the extremes from a political perspective, and you just take a look at what mainstream Loudoun County residents want, I think by and large you're going to find that they want SROs in elementary schools.

How we get there is the question, and I do like a phased in approach. I think it's reasonable, and I want to put that out there on the table as something that I definitely will be looking at. But I want to make sure also that we get this to a conclusion, that we get a document on the table that we can work with. If it's two separate or one combined, I don't know that I have a preference for either one, but I really would like us to see a very earnest effort in the next 30 days to get something

done. We've got to get this completed so that we're working under a current agreement that follows current law, and right now I'm worried that we're under an agreement while it's working fine, it doesn't actually fold in all the Thank you for coming out today and for providing your public comment. With that, we will move on to item number four, our memorandum of understanding between LCPS and law enforcement, including a new proposal from LCSO.

I just wanted to sort of level set before we start the discussion. Our item today is meant to be a discussion item, so it will be treated like a discussion item, information item. This is a perfect time to ask questions and to work through the process, but I don't foresee that any motions would be made today. We can discuss our plans for the next

meeting at the end of the meeting. But with that, we'll start this evening with a presentation from Ms. Ray Mitchell regarding the current status of the joint MOU. Thank you, Ms. Chandler. Good afternoon, members of the school board, Chair Chandler, LCSO, and LPD. This afternoon, I will be presenting a final draft version of the memorandum of

understanding between Loudoun County Public Schools, the Loudoun County Sheriff's Office, and the Leesburg Police Department. The current red line version of the MOU used the previously agreed upon MOU, which was executed in 2023, and which was updated with technical changes in 2024 to include updating names of the signing parties and editing punctuation as a starting place for discussion.

As mentioned in our previous select committee meeting, the three stakeholder agencies that collaborated to provide edits to the current red line version of the MOU are representatives from Loudoun County Public Schools, Loudoun County Sheriff's Office, and Leesburg Police Department. This process involved the members of each agency collaborating to provide input, align the document with Virginia Code where applicable, and review feedback from committees and the

public received during the feedback period, and to come to consensus regarding what changes would be made in the document. Portions of the current red line draft version of the MOU are those that are in all previous versions of the MOU, with the exception of three new sections, which were reviewed at the October 22nd select committee meeting.

This afternoon, I will provide some highlights of the edits that were made while showing portions of the MOU on the screen. We will begin with the preamble and purpose. In the current red line draft version of the MOU, starting with line nine, the preamble sets forth the respective roles and responsibilities of all parties

to include LCPS, LCSO, and LPD to maintain safe, supportive, and secure school environments. At line 32, the purpose of the MOU is to clarify the roles of SROs, school administration, and teachers, and outline expectations between the parties of LCPS, LCSO, and LPD,

as these parties work to foster a relationship of cooperation and mutual respect to maintain a safe and secure environment for students, staff, and visitors. Beginning at line 60, the MOU sets forth to clearly define the roles of all the parties. School resource officers, or SROs, is

defined in the Code of Virginia and who are assigned to schools who should operate under the MOU. Additional information regarding the various ways in which SROs support our middle and high schools will be provided as we move throughout the MOU. LCSO and LPD designate points of contact that will establish and maintain effective

relationships with school personnel, be responsible for the selection, assignment, scheduling, training, supervision, and evaluation of their respective personnel who serve as SROs. SROs receive a Department of Criminal Justice course as well as agency-defined training, and these trainings are listed beginning at line

102. Starting at lines 126 through 182, SROs serve in multiple roles and have responsibilities. They are expected to be familiar with the students' rights and responsibilities, exchange information with school administrators and LCPS safety and security

officers. They also provide a visible deterrent to crime and assist school administrators in developing school crisis management and response plans. SROs may also deliver law-related education to students, serve as informal mentors, and collaborate with school administrators when working with students with disabilities.

It is important to note that the feedback from the Special Education Advisory Committee, or SEAC, was considered and integrated into the MOU. Communication and collaboration between the administration and SRO will occur so that should a student require additional support, it can be provided. SROs receive training on the various types of disabilities, and LCPS has also

agreed to make training available to any SROs in order to support students with disabilities. It is the responsibility of the school division to ensure that each SRO is provided with a secure work area, that school administrators and teachers handle student discipline, and that the division communicates the goals and role of the SRO to all administration, staff, parents,

guardians, and students. LCPS, whose roles are clarified in the MOU starting at line 221, are that of the school administrator and safety and security officer. As school administrators, they are to review the MOU with SROs annually and report any reportable offenses to LCSO or LPD.

Safety and security officers, or SSOs, are LCPS employees who also work with school administration to help implement the division safety and security best practices and who are also DCJS certified prior to or within 60 days of the assignment in a school. Operationally, starting at line 256,

LCPS school officials have a direct responsibility for student behavior as well as school safety and security to cooperate with and report offenses to law enforcement authorities to the extent permitted by law, and when permissible, concurrently investigate allegations of violations of criminal laws committed on school property. Information sharing is governed by the Family Educational Rights

and Privacy Act, known as FERPA, which allows school officials to access and disclose student records for legitimate educational reasons. Access to real-time live video feed, which is a new section added to the MOU starting at line 306, outlines the instances when LCSO and LPD shall access real-time live video when there are

concerns for officer or fire official health and safety. All recorded images, video, and associated information shall be treated as confidential and is protected by state and federal law. The access to real-time live video shall be documented on a quarterly basis, and distribution of the information beyond LCSO and LPD is prohibited. However,

if there is an inadvertent third-party disclosure, LCPS division counsel must be informed immediately. SROs have the authority to question students or staff who may have information about criminal activities. Information regarding how that is conducted with juveniles or adult students and students with disabilities are outlined in the second appendix of the MOU, which will be referred to in a moment.

The actions of both law enforcement and LCPS administrators are aligned with Virginia Code and/or the students' rights and responsibilities. Body-worn cameras, or BWCs, at line 375, have been in use during previous school years. It was added as a new section to the MOU, and they are to be worn and used in accordance with applicable LCSO and LPD policies and procedures.

Cameras will only be activated during official law enforcement interactions. School searches and seizures are done in alignment with School Board Policy 8265, Searches Involving Students and Seizure of Contraband, which was updated in June of this year. While school officials may conduct searches and seize contraband, the SRO shall be contacted immediately to take custody

of any suspected illegal contraband. Otherwise, SROs shall not become involved in administrative school-related searches. Should an arrest be made, attempts to conduct the arrest are done outside of school hours and off of school grounds. However, there are instances when they must be done during school hours and/or on school grounds, and should that be the case, to the greatest extent

possible, there is coordination with the school administrator to minimize disruption. If physical intervention by the SRO is necessary, the action will be promptly reported to the school administrator and SRO supervisor with a documented rationale. Also, in alignment with LCPS Policy 5345, Restraint and Seclusion of Students,

which was updated in 2025, physical restraint is a last resort emergency procedure and should only be used if the student is in imminent danger to self or others. Other statutory responsibilities, which start at line 450, include crime reporting, threat assessment, school safety audits, and overdose notification.

Pursuant to the Code of Virginia, law enforcement agencies are required to notify a division superintendent, principal, or designee when a student in their school commits certain offenses. In alignment with School Board Policy 8290, Threat Assessment for the Protection of Schools, SROs are required members of a school's threat assessment team and

may assist in monitoring of students, and if needed, determine the need for any law enforcement action. School safety audits are conducted annually and meet all DCJS requirements to support school safety practices and conditions, and SROs are included in this process.

New in the red line version of the MOU, at line 489, is a section on overdose notification. LCPS has been following the guidance established by the Code of Virginia, where we are required to notify parents and guardians within 24 hours of a school suspected or confirmed overdose. A school suspected or school-connected student overdose is one for which the response is the administration of naloxone,

another opioid antagonist, or another similar medication with the intent to counter or temporarily reverse the effects of such overdose. Line 506 provides that the MOU shall be reviewed annually and amended or affirmed at least once every two years or at any time upon the request of either party.

There are two appendices in the MOU to clarify FERPA and student interview guidelines for law enforcement and school administrators. In the first appendix of the draft MOU, it was amended to remove the list of safety and emergency-related communications as they are detailed in Policy 3070.

In this appendix, it does outline in detail the parameters of when an SRO may access educational records in accordance with FERPA to include, but are not limited to, when there is a health or safety emergency, a report to Child Protective Services, or surveillance video.

Appendix two was largely amended to clarify the differences between juvenile and adult suspects, witnesses, or victims, and students with disabilities when needing to be questioned by law enforcement for offenses that occur on or off campus. As a juvenile suspect, the actions of the SRO are in alignment with Virginia Code, clarifying that they will attempt to

notify the parent or guardian and will notify the principal of an interview prior to questioning. For off-campus offenses, questioning shall only occur on school grounds if a delay may result in danger, destruction of evidence, or flight from the jurisdiction by the person suspected of having committed a criminal offense.
As with a juvenile suspect, the same information applies with notification to a parent or guardian for an on-campus offense, as well as when questioning shall occur for an off-campus offense.

The revisions in this portion of the appendix set forth to clarify when a student is recognized as an adult, and in such case, the SRO or law enforcement officer will not need to notify the student's parent or guardian of the interview. As with a student who is a juvenile, the same information applies for when there is questioning for an off-campus offense.

As with an adult suspect, the same information applies to adult witnesses or victims regarding the SRO or law enforcement officer not having to notify the parent or guardian, as well as when questioning shall occur for off-campus offenses. Regardless of whether a student with a disability is a suspect, witness, or victim, consideration will

be given on a case-by-case basis. If the student is a juvenile and has a disability, the parental notification will be provided in accordance with the juvenile students. If the student is an adult with a disability, the SRO is not required to make parental notification. Thank you, and this concludes the overall summary of the current red line version of the MOU. I will now turn it back over to Chair Chandler.

Thank you, Ms. Mitchell, for the overview. At this time, committee members, are there any questions? Okay. Then Lieutenant Colonel Sawyer, would you like to present the proposal by LCSO? So Sheriff Chapman has joined today, and I would like- Pardon me, Sheriff Chapman. It's so nice to see you. Thank you for being here. Sheriff Chapman, would you like to present your proposal? Yeah, absolutely.

First of all, thank you committee for having me here. Appreciate that, and Dr. Spence and the Loudoun County Public School staff, Leesburg Police and School Security and our community at large. I want to just go back on Ms. Mitchell's proposal, and all the items that are in there are in what we have also proposed, but let me get on with my remarks here. My job, as you know, is to keep our community safe.

Tonight I want to cover our school resource officer program and why we streamlined the MOU to conclude this process. I'd also like to explain our commitment to the children and their parents of this county, that we are here to keep everybody safe. First, our record of excellence. It's important that you know that we have a record of excellence for our children in our school environment, from elementary schools all the way up through high schools, and our record is second to none.

In 2018, our SRO program was recognized as only one of nine in the entire country by the National Association of School Resource Officers, NASRO, as a model program. That is amazing when you consider that there are over 6,000 law enforcement agencies nationwide with SROs. Loudoun County School Board recognized us as well with a proclamation that same year. This past April, NASRO recognized Senior Deputy Michael

Sennett with the Regional Exceptional Service Award. That's this year. He was one of 10 SROs out of 23,000 nationwide to receive this award. Our school resource officers were the first in the Commonwealth to mandate that all of our SROs were trained in crisis intervention. Our initiative prompted Virginia to mandate this training statewide. In elementary schools, we have taught D.A.R.E. since 1987. I was awarded the DEA D.A.R.E.

Executive of the Year Award in 2017 for our efforts in teaching our children about safety and making the right choices. Just this year, Deputy Robert Hefner was the only D.A.R.E. officer out of 22,000 nationwide to be named National D.A.R.E. Officer of the Year, and Master Deputy Phil Largent received D.A.R.E.'s Lifetime Achievement Award. With regards to our partnerships, our SROs in the Loudoun County Sheriff's Office

have an outstanding partnership with Loudoun County Public Schools. Our mandate at the Loudoun County Sheriff's Office is always to improve service, technology, efficiency, and professionalism. In doing this, common sense solutions almost always rise to the top. Unfortunately, the red line agreement, and I know there's a lot of work that went into this, I read it, I found it to be verbose, redundant, and desperate in need of streamlining. Considering that MOUs are a basic function of business,

and considering that we have over a decade of completing these agreements, a year and a half of writes and rewrites is beyond inefficient. It's ridiculous. And to tack on a select committee to delay the signing of this document even further is unconscionable. I sign probably a dozen various MOUs each year and have never seen such a process like this. This MOU is not a social experiment.

It's a document that simply defines our roles and responsibilities to keep our children, teachers, and administrators safe. It is modeled after the Department of Criminal Justice Services template. Pretty simple, at least it should be. Why I streamlined this. In reviewing the red line version, which inexplicably took a year and a half to get to that point, it was clear to me that this document could easily be cleaned up.

Consequently, I took the red line version, saw where the redundancies were, and took them out. There was no need to say the same thing two or three times. I followed the DCJS format, which we have always done. All the changes proposed in the red line version were kept. Everything that's in there has been kept. There are only two changes that I made. The first was to provide the correct language which defines SROs in the Code of

Virginia, which states, quote, "A certified law enforcement officer hired by a local law enforcement agency to provide law enforcement and security services to Virginia elementary and secondary schools." The other change I made was to remove the Leesburg Police Department from our agreement with the schools to allow them to have their own separate agreement with the school board. Considering both agencies have different reporting structures, attorneys, and

exist within different bureaucracies, this will enable either agency to resolve any issues they may experience directly with Loudoun County Public Schools, instead of attempting to come to some type of a three-way resolution. After circulating this through my executive staff for input and coming to a clean, almost final version, I had our county attorney's office review this document. A few final edits were made, and that was the final version of what I provided Dr. Spence last week.

We have already proven that we can make this process work when it comes to MOUs. When the county recently opened its new crisis receiving center, the Loudoun County Sheriff's Office and Leesburg Police Department each signed individual MOUs with the center. This was accomplished in less than two months, not a year and a half. Elementary schools. Briefly on elementary schools, and every middle school and high school in Loudoun County has a full-time Elementary school. Our elementary schools do not.

Full-time SRO, our elementary schools do not. Last school year, SROs pulled from their own middle and high schools and answered 1,340 calls at elementary schools. So far this school year, there have been 11 school shootings nationwide with injuries or deaths as reported by Education Week. Two of those were elementary schools, which tracks with longstanding data that about 20% of all school shootings occur at elementary schools.

About four weeks ago, as we all know, in Bend, Oregon, three children and a teacher were killed at Silver Rail Elementary School. That district assigned SROs only to its high schools and two middle schools. After the shooting, it placed an SRO at Silver Rail, and more than 3,000 people signed a petition asking for an SRO in every school. Here in Loudoun, we had approximately 200 threat assessments in

elementary schools alone last year, and have had about 50 so far this school year. So this is what is obviously also wanted by the citizens of Loudoun County. We have three media surveys that have shown that between 60% and 70% of the people that responded to these surveys are in favor of elementary school SROs. So I'd like to close my remarks by discussing elementary school SROs.

I understand this issue came up in the last meeting here with your committee, and I'd like to mention a few things here. My ask is that we work together and at least start a pilot program. I believe we had talked about, and we'd even talked about this in the past, about starting with clusters. Not to fund everyone, not to fund every elementary school in the county, but to do it in clusters,

monitor it, and see how that goes, and see where we go from there. You may notice that the proposed draft of the SRO coverage as agreed upon between the sheriff's office, rather than limiting it to middle and high schools, we've put that in there because that's what the law states. That's what the Code of Virginia states. It's between middle, elementary, and secondary schools. And what we can do here is,

whether we go in that direction or not, we're covered either way. That change is important as we have the flexibility to begin a program without having to draft another MOU that would cover elementary schools. To close, I want to simply ensure that our youngest students have the same protection we already give their older brothers and sisters. It's important that everybody, from children on up, and I think we have a record that shows that.

When you look at everything that we've done, the successes that we've had in elementary schools, there is no threat. The people love them. We have an outstanding DARE program. I think that reflects well in elementary schools. The community loves it. If they didn't, we wouldn't still have it. They absolutely love that program, and it just shows the connection that we have with the children in those schools and the relationship we have with the school, with the students, the staff, the teachers, and the

administrators, and the parents of those schools. So these are the things that we need to capitalize on to make sure that we keep everybody in this county safe. Thank you. Thank you, Sheriff Chapman. Committee members, any questions? Yes, Vice Chair Donahue. Thank you, Madam Chair. Thank you for being here, Sheriff Chapman. I appreciate the opportunity to have conversations with you directly about the MOU and your request for elementary school SROs.

I have several questions. Your proposed MOU references numerous times the Virginia School Law Enforcement Partnership guide. So I assume you're familiar with that document and its contents. Yes. So I have a few questions related to that document. So first of all, the SLEP guide on page 19 suggests that the parties to an MOU have quarterly meetings throughout the year to gauge how the program is going.

Is that something that's been happening currently between LCSO and LCPS? Okay. I don't know if we have quarterly meetings, but I can tell you every year, I know we meet with John Clark, with the security people here. We go through everything that's expected of our SROs and everybody in all of the middle and high schools there. And as far as quarterly meetings go, I don't know. Do you know, Chris?

So I don't know that there's formal structured quarterly meetings that are occurring. I do know that there's constant communication between LCPS administration and our SRO unit and the staff there. And when you say administration, Colonel Sawyer, you mean Mr. Clark? Just for purposes of my clarity. So I would say on a couple different levels. From a school security side, Mr. Clark, for sure. But there's also significant communication with the chief of schools, Dr. Mitchell. Okay. Thank you.

I also was wondering if LCSO tracks use of force incidents which are alleged to be perpetrated by SROs while they're executing their responsibilities as SROs. I'm sorry, do we track what? Use of force incidents by SROs. We track all use of force incidents by every deputy in the Loudoun County Sheriff's Office. Is that information publicly available? We do an annual report. Yeah. Go ahead. You take it. We tried to find it on your website and weren't able to do so.

So I'd like to know if that information's publicly available. Sure. So there is an annual report published on our website related to all of our internal affairs investigations use of force. And does that include a category for SROs? I don't believe there's a breakout specifically for SROs. I do know use of force in schools is extremely rare Have you seen any incidents of that? Are you aware of any excessive use of forces in an elementary school? I'd like to know, Sheriff Chapman, if your office is following the law, because

Virginia code requires that you keep track of those statistics and make them readily available. I know my question is, if there's a report of that, we would certainly investigate it. So of course, we investigate every use of force and with all of our deputies, no matter where they are. So my next question, Sheriff Chapman, is on the section of your MOU that refers to required training for SROs, in which you have listed cultural diversity awareness under as one of the bullets. However, you have left out systemic

and individual racism and implicit bias, which is recovered by code. Why did you remove that language? We can adjust that if we want to keep it exactly to the code like everything else is there. I'm happy to adjust that and put the exact code reference in there. But can you tell me why you decided to remove that language? I thought the language was excessive, but we can certainly put that in there since it's part of the Virginia code.

I'm also curious why you removed, there was language in the red line draft related to the LCPS policy change related to restraint seclusion, that says that seclusion is now an impermissible practice in LCPS, and that has been removed. Can you explain why you removed that language? Sorry, can you state that section again?
Supporting students with disabilities. It's on page four of the red line. I don't think we left that out.

I have another question related to that section as well, because the last line there says, "LCPS will also provide additional disability training to SROs as available," and I was hoping that you could explain to me what you mean by that, because Colonel Sawyer explained previously, we cannot compel SROs to take any particular types of training. So what does this mean, LCPS will also provide additional disability training?

While Lieutenant Colonel Sawyer is looking that up, I can tell you that we provide constant training to our people. They have more training than our deputies in the field when it comes to dealing with students, and we're always looking at ways to improve that training and capitalize on other opportunities for training. So, I can't tell you every training scenario or every training session everybody has been through, but I can tell you that we take a lot of pride in the amount of training.

And I think when you look at the fact that we have received all these recognitions and awards for the service that we provide, the reputation that we have when it comes to SROs, and the fact that we were the first people to even have crisis intervention training with our SROs, shows that we're on the front side of this issue, not on the back side of it. So specific to the line on training, and I'd asked you to go back to the other one, I'm still trying to find the other one. But specific to the line on training,

that was essentially a rewording of the line of, I have it on my copy as line 197 of the red line document, that said, "LCPS will make available to all SROs any training on supporting students with disabilities." So the line in that section is basically a reword of that, that LCSO will also provide additional disability training to SROs as available. I'm thrilled for LCPS to be providing training if LCSO

is willing to accept it. Just we've been told previously that we cannot compel you to take specific training, so I wanted to be clear what you envision to be LCPS' responsibilities under this document. So I have another question. I'm looking at the section on school administrator roles and responsibilities in Sheriff Chapman's

version of the MOU. There's a line in here that I believe is new that says, "Misdemeanor offenses should also be shared and discussed with the SRO to ensure an accurate overall picture of the school climate." Is that our current practice? I don't think we changed that. And if that question is better directed to- Can you do me a favor and tell us exactly where in both documents,

where you have that in the document and how it's different from the document that we have? How it's different? It is a sentence that you added, Sheriff Chapman, under school administrator roles and responsibilities, that is not in the red line that we've been working on for a year and a half, that says, "Misdemeanor offenses should also be shared and discussed with the SRO to ensure an accurate

overall picture of the school climate." If that is not currently our present practice to report misdemeanor offenses, I would like to know why you chose to add this language. So that is the present practice. I can answer that. So when we talk about misdemeanors, misdemeanors are also school fights. So if a kid gets into a fight and a misdemeanor assault, the principal will inform the SRO that the misdemeanor assault did occur, and the majority of the time, the school will handle discipline.

A lot of times the reason for that is because if the parents do want to pursue charges, then they will then go to that SRO and talk to them with them Same thing when it comes to vapes, same thing when it comes to larcenies, all those different misdemeanor things that happen in schools. The principals already do contact the SROs and tell them what's going on there. So that is a practice. I appreciate that clarification. So it sounds like I was right that that is not our current practice, and also it's not required by Virginia Code, so we could choose to

agree to that if that is the will of LCPS and this board. Although- So- I-- Yes, Colonel Sawyer? Sorry. If I can add, that is actually in the existing document. It is under the school administrator roles and responsibilities. On my copy, it's line 239. The paragraph starts with all reportable offenses, and it lists the code section,

where it says, at the end of 239, "Further misdemeanor offenses should also be shared and discussed with the SRO to ensure an accurate overall picture of the school climate." So that's in the existing signed. That's not a red line change. That's the- So Colonel Sawyer, my understanding is that that is language that LCSO had previously proposed adding into this and that we struck out. So on my printout, I see that sentence on line 238, but it has been struck through, because I believe it
was our preference to not include that language because it was not in the previous version.

I have a couple of additional questions. Next, in the information sharing section, this document very clearly and specifically states SROs are not designated school officials for LCPS. However, again, in the Virginia School Law Enforcement Partnership Guide on page 17, that document explicitly states that SROs are
